entry.title: OAuth, Authentication vs Authorization, and Google Login in Next.js

link.title: OAuth, Authentication vs Authorization, and Google Login in Next.js

entry.content:
Login, OAuth, authentication, and authorization get used as if they mean the same thing. They do not, and treating them as one idea is how you end up with an app that can sign someone in but has no clear answer for what that person is allowed to do.

In this post I will cover the concepts first, then the practical piece:

  • What authentication and authorization actually mean
  • What OAuth is, what it is not, and how OpenID Connect fits in
  • What roles Okta and Google play
  • Which library I would use to add Google Login to a Next.js app
  • How to set that integration up, including the operational details that usually cause the first outage

If you are about to drop a “Sign in with Google” button into a Next.js app, it helps to know what that button is doing before you copy a snippet into app/.

Authentication vs authorization

Authentication answers one question: who is this?

Authorization answers a different question: what is this person allowed to do?

A familiar ops example is a Linux box. Logging in with your SSH key is authentication. The server now knows which user you are. Being listed in sudoers, having access to a particular database role, or being allowed through a security group is authorization. You can authenticate successfully and still be denied the action you wanted.

The same split shows up everywhere:

  • A badge getting you through the front door is authentication. The badge reader on the server room is authorization.
  • A valid AWS console login is authentication. An IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject on one bucket and denies everything else is authorization.
  • A valid session cookie in a web app means the app knows who you are. A role, group, feature flag, or ownership check decides whether you can see a customer record or trigger a deploy.

People shorten both of these to “auth,” which is where the confusion starts. In conversation that shorthand is fine. In a system design it is not. If you only implement authentication, every signed-in user looks the same. If you only think about authorization, you have no reliable way to know who the actor is.

A few consequences that matter in real applications:

  • Authentication should happen as little as you can get away with. The user proves who they are, you establish a session, and you reuse that session.
  • Authorization should happen often. Every protected page, API route, and server action needs to ask whether this user can do this thing.
  • A successful login is not a permission grant. “They signed in with Google” does not mean they should see admin pages, other users’ data, or Google Drive files they never agreed to share.

When someone says “we need to add auth,” it is worth asking which half they mean. Sometimes they want a login button. Sometimes they want SSO for employees. Sometimes they want fine-grained permissions. Those are different designs.

What OAuth actually is

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. It exists so a user can grant your application limited access to an account they already have, without giving you their password.

That last part is the original point. Before OAuth, a third-party app that needed access to your Google data would ask for your Google password. That is a terrible design. OAuth replaces “give me your password” with “send the user to Google, let Google ask for consent, then give the app a token that only covers what the user approved.”

OAuth has a few standard roles, and the names are worth knowing because they show up in every provider’s docs:

  • The resource owner is the user.
  • The client is your application.
  • The authorization server is the system that authenticates the user and issues tokens. For Google Login, this is Google. For a company SSO setup, it is often Okta.
  • The resource server is the API being accessed. That might be Gmail or Drive, or it might be your own API if you are validating tokens yourself.

The authorization code flow

The flow you should use for a server-side Next.js app is the authorization code flow.

  1. The user clicks “Sign in with Google” in your app.
  2. Your app redirects them to Google, along with your client ID, a redirect URI, and the scopes you want.
  3. Google authenticates the user if they are not already signed in. That step is authentication, and it happens on Google’s side, not in your app.
  4. Google shows a consent screen if needed, so the user can approve what your app is asking for.
  5. Google redirects the user back to your app with a short-lived authorization code.
  6. Your server exchanges that code for tokens, using your client secret. This exchange happens server-to-server, which is why the user’s browser never needs to see the client secret.
  7. Your app receives tokens and can now either create a local session, call a Google API, or both.

If you have been around long enough, you may remember the implicit flow, where tokens were returned directly in the URL fragment. Do not use that. The authorization code flow is the current standard, and public clients should also use PKCE so an intercepted code cannot be exchanged by someone else. A Next.js app with a server-side route handler is a confidential client because it can keep a client secret. You should still treat that secret like any other production credential.

What the tokens mean

  • An access token is authorization. It lets your app call an API within the scopes the user approved. It is usually short-lived.
  • A refresh token lets your app request a new access token later without sending the user through the consent screen every time. Google typically issues a refresh token only the first time the user consents, unless you force a new consent prompt.
  • An ID token comes from OpenID Connect (OIDC), which sits on top of OAuth 2.0. The ID token is a signed assertion of identity: subject identifier, email, name, and similar claims. That is how a Google sign-in becomes authentication for your app, not just permission to call Google’s APIs.

This distinction matters. If you only needed to read a user’s Google Calendar, you would care about OAuth scopes and an access token. If you need a logged-in session in your own Next.js app, you care about the identity information and how you turn that into a session you control.

Scopes are authorization decisions

Scopes are the permissions your app is requesting. They are easy to treat as a boilerplate list, but they are an authorization decision the user has to approve.

For Google Login, the identity scopes are usually enough:

  • openid
  • email
  • profile

That combination tells Google you want to know who the user is. It does not give you access to Gmail, Drive, Calendar, or anything else in their Google account.

If your app later needs Drive access, that is a separate authorization request. Do not bake https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file into the original login just because you might want it someday. Users are more likely to abandon a consent screen that asks for more than the app is obviously doing, and you should not be holding unused grants.

What OAuth is not

A few things OAuth is often mistaken for:

  • It is not a login protocol by itself. Login is the OIDC layer on top, or a session your app creates after it trusts the identity token.
  • It is not a permissions system for your own application data. Google can tell you who the user is, and it can authorize access to Google APIs. It does not know whether that user should edit invoice 123 in your database.
  • It does not replace session handling. After the callback, you still need a session, cookie, or token strategy in your own app.
  • It does not mean you should store Google access tokens in localStorage or log them. Treat them like secrets.

Two operational details that cause most first-time failures:

  • Redirect URIs must match exactly, including scheme, host, path, and trailing slash. Google will reject the request with redirect_uri_mismatch if they do not.
  • Client secrets belong on the server, in environment variables, not in frontend code or git.

Where Okta and Google fit

Google and Okta can both act as an identity provider. In an OAuth/OIDC flow, your app does not collect the user’s password. It redirects the user to the provider, the provider authenticates them, and your app receives tokens it can verify.

They overlap, but they are usually used for different jobs.

Google

For most public apps, Google means Sign in with Google. The user already has a Google account. Your app does not want to store another password. Google authenticates the user and returns identity information through OIDC. If you requested API scopes, Google also returns access tokens that authorize calls to those Google APIs.

Google also appears in company environments through Google Workspace. In that case Google is still the identity provider, but the accounts belong to the organization. You can restrict sign-in to a Workspace domain, which is useful for internal tools. That restriction is an authorization policy sitting on top of Google authentication: “they must be a Google user, and they must belong to this domain.”

So Google can play two related roles:

  • As an identity provider, it answers who the user is.
  • As an authorization server for Google APIs, it answers whether your app may call Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and similar services on that user’s behalf.

What Google does not do, at least not by default, is manage the permissions inside your product. It will not tell you who an admin is in your SaaS app, which tenants they belong to, or whether they can approve a payroll run.

Okta

Okta is usually the enterprise identity layer. Companies use it for workforce SSO, MFA, user lifecycle, and deciding which applications a person can open. In that setup, employees do not sign into each internal tool separately. They sign into Okta, and Okta issues tokens your apps trust.

Okta can authenticate users itself with a password plus MFA, passwordless options, or similar. It can also federate to another provider, including Google. That is a common pattern: the employee clicks into an internal app, lands on Okta, and Okta may then send them to Google Workspace to prove who they are. From your app’s point of view, Okta is still the identity provider. Your app should validate Okta’s tokens, not talk to Google directly.

On the authorization side, Okta is often the source of truth for groups, roles, and application assignments. A user might be in an engineering group and assigned to your app, or they might be authenticated but not assigned to that app at all. Okta can also act as an OAuth authorization server for your own APIs, issuing access tokens with scopes and claims your backend can enforce.

Okta also has a customer-identity side, where it provides login, social identity, and related features for an application’s end users rather than employees. The same building blocks show up there: authentication at Okta, tokens for your app, and policies for who can access what.

How to choose

A simple way to think about it:

  • If you are building a public or customer-facing Next.js app and you want low-friction login, Google Login is a common fit. The user already has an account, and you do not need to become a password database on day one.
  • If you are building an internal or enterprise app and the company already lives in Okta, Okta should be the identity provider. Users may still reach Okta via Google, but your app should trust Okta.
  • You can use both. Okta can sit in front as the SSO broker, with Google as one of the ways a user proves who they are.
  • If you need Google API access, that is a Google OAuth problem even if login itself goes through Okta. Those are separate grants.

Neither product replaces the original distinction. Google or Okta can authenticate someone. Your application still has to decide what that person is authorized to do once they are in. Sometimes that decision is as simple as “any signed-in user can see their own dashboard.” Sometimes it is groups from Okta, a role stored in your database, or an email-domain check. Make that decision explicit.

Which library I would use in Next.js

For a new Next.js app that needs Google Login, I would use Better Auth.

For a long time, the default answer was NextAuth.js, later renamed Auth.js. It still works, and if you already have it in production there is no reason to rip it out just to chase a newer name. The Auth.js project is now maintained by the Better Auth team, and they recommend starting new projects with Better Auth unless you have a specific gap.

Why Better Auth is the better default today:

  • It is self-hosted and configured in code. That fits a DevOps workflow better than dropping in a hosted auth product before you need one.
  • Google is a built-in social provider, so you are not writing the OAuth handshake, token exchange, or callback handling by hand.
  • Users, sessions, and linked accounts live in a database you control.
  • The Next.js integration is small: a catch-all API route plus a client helper.
  • Features you often need later, such as additional social providers or stronger session handling, are already part of the same system instead of a pile of one-off packages.

A few alternatives, if the requirements are different:

  • Auth.js / NextAuth if the app already uses it and it is stable. Leave it alone until you have a concrete reason to migrate.
  • Clerk or a similar hosted service if you want login working quickly and you are comfortable with user records living in someone else’s system.
  • Okta’s own SDK if Okta is your identity provider. Do not run Google Login and Okta side by side as two sources of truth for the same users.
  • Rolling your own OAuth client is possible, but you will spend time on redirect handling, CSRF, token storage, session cookies, and edge cases that a maintained library already covers. I would not start there unless I had a very specific constraint.

The rest of this post assumes a new Next.js app that should sign users in with Google, using Better Auth.

How to add Google Login to a Next.js app

This is the hands-on path I would take. The Google Cloud setup is where most of the friction is. The library code itself is fairly small.

Step 1: Configure the Google OAuth client

In Google Cloud Console:

  1. Create or select a project.
  2. Configure the OAuth consent screen if you have not already. For a side project you can start in testing mode and add your own Google account as a test user. For an internal Workspace app, an internal consent screen avoids the external verification process.
  3. Go to APIs & Services → Credentials.
  4. Create an OAuth client ID and choose Web application.
  5. Add authorized JavaScript origins:
    • http://localhost:3000
    • https://your-domain.com
  6. Add authorized redirect URIs:
    • Local: http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/google
    • Production: https://your-domain.com/api/auth/callback/google
  7. Copy the client ID and client secret.

A few things that are easy to miss:

  • Localhost and production are different redirect URIs. You need both registered before you deploy, or production login will fail even though local login worked.
  • The path has to match what the library expects. Better Auth’s default callback is /api/auth/callback/google. If you change the auth base path, update Google Cloud to match.
  • http versus https matters. So does www versus the apex domain. So does a trailing slash.
  • The client secret is a secret. Do not commit it, paste it into a frontend file, or drop it into a screenshot.

If the redirect URI does not match, Google returns redirect_uri_mismatch. That error almost always means the callback your app is sending does not match what you registered, or BETTER_AUTH_URL is still pointing at localhost after deploy.

Step 2: Install Better Auth and set environment variables

npm install better-auth better-sqlite3

SQLite is enough to prove the flow locally. Before you take this to production, switch to Postgres or whatever database you already run, using one of Better Auth’s adapters.

Add the following to .env:

BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=  # openssl rand -base64 32
BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3000
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=

BETTER_AUTH_SECRET should be a long random value. You can generate one with:

openssl rand -base64 32

BETTER_AUTH_URL should be the public URL of the app. Locally that is http://localhost:3000. In production it should be your real HTTPS origin. Better Auth uses this value to construct the callback URL it sends to Google, so a wrong value here looks exactly like a misconfigured redirect URI.

Keep these variables out of git. If you deploy to AWS Amplify, add them in the Amplify console for that app and environment rather than baking them into the build output. I wrote about deploying a Next.js app to Amplify separately; the important part here is that production needs its own BETTER_AUTH_URL and its own Google redirect URI.

Then generate or apply the Better Auth schema:

npx auth@latest migrate

Better Auth needs somewhere to store users, sessions, and the linked Google account. The migrate step creates that schema. If you are using an ORM adapter, use the generate flow from the Better Auth docs and review the migration before you apply it.

Step 3: Create the auth config

Create lib/auth.ts:

import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";
import { nextCookies } from "better-auth/next-js";
import Database from "better-sqlite3";

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: new Database("./sqlite.db"),
  baseURL: process.env.BETTER_AUTH_URL,
  socialProviders: {
    google: {
      clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID as string,
      clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET as string,
    },
  },
  plugins: [nextCookies()],
});

A few notes on that file:

  • baseURL is not optional in practice. If it is missing or still set to localhost in production, Google will reject the callback.
  • nextCookies() should stay last in the plugin list so cookies are set correctly when you call auth methods from server actions.
  • This config only requests Google as a login provider. You are not asking for Drive, Gmail, or other Google API scopes yet.

If you later need to force account selection every time, Better Auth lets you set prompt: "select_account" on the Google provider. That is useful on a shared machine, or when you are testing with more than one Google account.

If this is an internal app and only one Workspace domain should be allowed in, set hd to that domain on the provider. That is an authorization rule: authenticated Google users outside the domain should not get a session.

Step 4: Mount the Next.js route handler

Create app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts:

import { auth } from "@/lib/auth";
import { toNextJsHandler } from "better-auth/next-js";

export const { GET, POST } = toNextJsHandler(auth);

This catch-all route is the callback endpoint Google redirects to, and it also handles the rest of the auth API. You generally want to leave it at /api/auth/[...all] unless you have a reason to change the base path. If you do change it, update the Google Cloud redirect URI and BETTER_AUTH_URL handling to match.

Step 5: Add a Sign in with Google button

Create lib/auth-client.ts:

import { createAuthClient } from "better-auth/react";

export const authClient = createAuthClient();

Then a small client component:

"use client";

import { authClient } from "@/lib/auth-client";

export function GoogleSignInButton() {
  return (
    <button
      onClick={() =>
        authClient.signIn.social({
          provider: "google",
        })
      }
    >
      Sign in with Google
    </button>
  );
}

When the user clicks the button, they are redirected to Google, they approve the login, and they come back to your app with a session. Signing out is the other half of that client:

await authClient.signOut();

At this point you have the OAuth/OIDC round trip working: Google authenticated the user, your app received identity information, and Better Auth created a local session.

Step 6: Read the session on the server

Do not treat “there is a cookie” as proof that someone is signed in. Checking for a cookie is fine as a fast redirect hint, but any protected page or server action should validate the session on the server.

import { auth } from "@/lib/auth";
import { headers } from "next/headers";
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";

export default async function DashboardPage() {
  const session = await auth.api.getSession({
    headers: await headers(),
  });

  if (!session) {
    redirect("/sign-in");
  }

  return <h1>Welcome {session.user.name}</h1>;
}

That check is authentication: is there a valid session, and who does it belong to? It is not yet authorization. Once you have session.user, you can add the rules that belong to your product:

  • Only users with an email on your company domain can continue.
  • Only users marked as admins can open /admin.
  • A user can only read rows that belong to their account or tenant.

Those checks should live in the server code that performs the action, not only in the navigation UI. Hiding a button is not authorization.

If you use Next.js middleware or, on newer versions, a proxy file to redirect anonymous users, treat that as an optimistic check. Better Auth’s own docs are explicit that looking at the session cookie is not a security boundary. Always validate the session again in the page, route handler, or server action.

Step 7: Keep login separate from Google API access

After login works, it is tempting to add more Google scopes to the same button. I would not do that by default.

Login should ask for identity. Extra access should be requested when a feature actually needs it. Better Auth can request additional Google scopes later through linkSocial, for example if the user clicks “Connect Google Drive.” That triggers a new consent flow for those scopes instead of surprising people on day one.

This is the OAuth-versus-login distinction again, in product form. Signing the user in is authentication. Reading their Drive files is authorization for a Google API, and it deserves its own consent.

What “done” looks like in production

A local demo is not the same as a login system you can leave running. Before you call this finished, walk through the operational checklist:

  • Production redirect URIs are registered in Google Cloud, not just localhost.
  • BETTER_AUTH_URL in production is the public HTTPS origin.
  • BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET are set in the hosting environment and not checked into the repo.
  • The database is not a leftover SQLite file on a local disk. Use a real database, back it up, and run schema changes through your normal migration process.
  • HTTPS is required in production. OAuth callbacks and secure cookies depend on it.
  • You have tested sign-in, sign-out, and a second sign-in with the same Google account. The second visit should find the existing user rather than create a duplicate.
  • You have tested the failure path: canceling the Google consent screen should not leave the app in a broken state.
  • If the app is internal, confirm that accounts outside the allowed domain cannot get a session.

If login works locally and fails after deploy, start with the callback URL. In my experience that is the first thing to inspect, before you assume the library is misbehaving.

Wrapping up

A short recap:

  • Authentication is who you are. Authorization is what you can do. A successful login only solves the first one.
  • OAuth is an authorization framework for delegated access. It lets a user grant your app limited access without sharing a password.
  • “Sign in with Google” uses OAuth plus OpenID Connect. The ID token is how Google tells your app who the user is. Access tokens and scopes are how Google authorizes API calls.
  • Google is a common identity provider for social login and Google Workspace, and it is also the authorization server for Google APIs. Okta is typically the enterprise SSO and policy layer. They can work together, but your app should have one source of truth for identity.
  • For a new Next.js app, I would use Better Auth, create a Google OAuth client, and add Google Login through Better Auth’s Google social provider. Then I would enforce authorization in the application itself.

Once this is in place, the next useful step is deciding how permissions should work after login: an email-domain restriction, roles in your own database, or claims and groups from an identity provider such as Okta. That is a separate design from the login button, and it is the part most apps need to think about sooner than they expect.

entry.title: Running OpenClaw on a Cloud Node

link.title: Running OpenClaw on a Cloud Node

entry.content:
OpenClaw

OpenClaw is an open-source AI assistant framework that runs on infrastructure you control. Instead of depending on a hosted AI agent service, you can deploy it on a small VPS and keep your models, tools, and data flow closer to your own environment.

In this post, I will focus on a practical question: why run OpenClaw on a cloud node, and what does a minimal secure setup look like on a low-cost VPS such as Hetzner or AWS Lightsail?

Why run it on a cloud node?

Running OpenClaw on a VPS is useful if you want:

  • Always-on availability: Your assistant stays online even when your laptop is closed.
  • Stable network reachability: Easier remote access, webhooks, and gateway access than on a home network.
  • Separation from your daily machine: Agent tooling, logs, and automations live on a dedicated host.
  • Predictable cost: A small instance is often enough for a personal agent, especially if inference happens through external model APIs.

What is OpenClaw?

OpenClaw is a personal AI agent platform built for developers and power users. Key traits:

  • Self-hosted: Runs on your hardware (laptop, server, Raspberry Pi, or cloud node).
  • Messaging integrations: Can connect to services like WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, and others through its gateway and integrations.
  • Agentic: Supports subagents, tools (file ops, shell exec, web search), skills (plugins for GitHub, calendars, etc.), and persistent memory.
  • Model-agnostic: Works with hosted and local models, depending on your provider setup.
  • Open-source: GitHub repo with a large and active community.

It’s not just a chatbot; it’s an extensible system for automation, with heartbeats for proactivity, cron jobs, and community skills.

What Can It Do?

OpenClaw shines in real-world automation:

  • Task automation: Clear inboxes, manage calendars (gcalcli), send emails, check flights.
  • Development workflows: GitHub issues/PRs (skills like gh-issues), code review, CI monitoring.
  • Research & content: Web search, image gen/analysis, note-taking (Obsidian publish).
  • System ops: Shell access (safe exec), file management, tmux control.
  • Proactive: Heartbeats check emails/calendar/weather; subagents for parallel tasks.
  • Voice/media: TTS, image handling, voice notes transcription.

Examples: “Ship checklist” can become an automated deployment checklist, or you can spawn subagents for parallel work across multiple repos.

Security Considerations

Self-hosting improves control, but it also means you own the operational risk:

  • Minimal exposure: Prefer loopback-only binding plus Tailscale or another private access layer instead of opening the gateway publicly.
  • Secrets handling: Store API keys carefully and keep them out of shell history, screenshots, and public dotfiles.
  • Exec safety: Treat shell and file tools as privileged capabilities. Keep approval requirements in place for destructive or elevated commands.
  • Firewalling: Allow only what you need, ideally SSH and your private networking layer.
  • Updates: Stay current with OpenClaw and its runtime requirements.
  • Isolation: Run as a non-root user and keep the workspace scoped to what the agent actually needs.
  • Plugin hygiene: Review skills and plugins before enabling them on a machine with real data.

The main risks are straightforward: prompt injection, accidental over-permissioning, and exposing an interface to the public internet without enough access control.

Practical Setup on Hetzner or AWS Lightsail

  1. Provision node:
    • Hetzner: a small shared vCPU instance with Ubuntu 24.04 is enough to start.
    • Lightsail: a small Ubuntu instance is also fine for a personal deployment.
    • Create a non-root user and use SSH keys.
  2. Secure basics: 
    sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install ufw curl -y
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow ssh
sudo ufw --force enable
# Disable root SSH, password auth in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo systemctl restart ssh
  3. Install Node & OpenClaw: 
    curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash
openclaw onboard --install-daemon

    OpenClaw currently recommends Node 24, with Node 22.16+ also supported if you are installing through npm instead of the installer script.

  4. Configure & pair:
    • Pair the channels you actually use, such as WhatsApp or Telegram.
    • Set your model provider and workspace during onboarding.
    • Test: openclaw agent --message "Hello from cloud!".
  5. Remote access (optional):
    • Tailscale is a good fit if you want private remote access without exposing the gateway directly to the internet.
    • Keep the gateway bound to loopback where possible and let Tailscale handle access.
  6. Monitor: openclaw doctor, journalctl -u openclaw (systemd).

At that point you have an always-on OpenClaw node with a cleaner separation between your assistant runtime and your personal machine.

entry.title: Folder Automation on a Mac Using Automator

link.title: Folder Automation on a Mac Using Automator

entry.content:
Introduction

We will be using ImageMagick and the Mac Automator to help us more easily do a common image conversion task. This can be useful if you commonly need to reduce image sizes for publishing to the web or for doing common conversions from one file type to another. The end result will be a process where you can simply drop a file in a folder and it will automatically do the conversion.

We will be using ImageMagick to process the files and a custom script to run it.

Steps

  • Install ImageMagick:
brew install imagemagick

# Confirm that magick command works
magick -help
  • Next, using the Mac Finder, create a folder for your automation. Let’s call it image_edit. Inside of the image_edit folder, create an input and an output folder. The automation will run when we drop a file in the input folder, and the automation will then place the edited file in the output folder.
  • Use Spotlight Search (Command-Space) to find Automator.

  • Once opened, select File / New and then select folder action

  • Find the dropdown at the top labeled Folder Action receives files and folders added to. Use the dropdown to select the input folder that was created.

  • In the search field, type shell to easily find the Run Shell Script action. Drag it over to the Main section of the window.

  • Keep the Shell as /bin/zsh and change the Pass input to as arguments. At this stage, the automator may show an example script within the action as shown:

  • Create a shell script in the image_edit folder that will edit the image. In our case, we will have the script run ImageMagick on the image to have it with a specific quality and dimension, and to have it standardized as a JPG. Regardless of the format you drop in the folder, ImageMagick will attempt to make the adjustments and save the file as a JPG.
#!/bin/sh

# The variable '$f' will hold the path to the file that was added.
for f in "$@"
do
	# Add echo command to validate the automation is running
    echo "$(date): New file added: $f" >> ~/Documents/folder_action_log.txt

    # Get the base filename without the extension
    filename=$(basename "$f")
    name_no_ext="${filename%.*}"
    output_file="$HOME/Documents/Scripts/image_edit/output/${name_no_ext}.jpg"

	# Use more echo commands for troubleshooting only
    echo "output_file: $output_file" >> ~/Documents/folder_action_log.txt
    echo "name_no_ext: $name_no_ext" >> ~/Documents/folder_action_log.txt
    echo "filename: $filename" >> ~/Documents/folder_action_log.txt

	# Run ImageMagick with desired options and delete original file
    /opt/homebrew/bin/magick "$f" -strip -quality 90 -resize 1024x628\> "$output_file"
    rm -f "$f"

done
  • After the shell script has been created, you can now tell Automator where the script is located and add a placeholder for the arguments. Automator will use the full file name (using a full path) for the argument. Example:

  • In the Finder, go to the input folder and select Services and then Folder Actions Setup.

  • Select Run Service if a pop up appears.
  • Choose a script to attach. Attach the script from the list shown.
  • You should see the folder name and the script name in the Folder Actions Setup window.

Test and Troubleshoot

Test the automation by dropping an image in the input folder. You should see a new file created in the output folder and the input folder file should disappear. Notice that the sample script provided will use echo commands to send output to a file. This can be very helpful during testing to make sure that the script is running properly. You may want to remove those commands once the script is working properly to avoid having a huge log file.

entry.title: Changing DNS Service Providers
entry.content:
Changing DNS Service Providers

Changing form one DNS registrar to another can seem like a major undertaking with risks such as taking down your web property for an extended period of time. If done improperly, it is possible you could take your site down for several hours while DNS propagates. Migrating a DNS out of a DNS registrar (for example GoDaddy or HostGator) involves two main steps: move the DNS records over and then after propagation has completed, move over the domain itself.

We will be following an example of moving a domain out of HostGator and into AWS Route 53.

Migrating DNS Records

  • Create a Hosted Zone in AWS Route 53
    • Go to Route 53 → Hosted Zones → Create a new public hosted zone for the domain you are moving.
    • Route 53 will give you 4 NS (Name Server) records (like ns-123.awsdns-45.org).
  • Gather all DNS Records from HostGator
    • Log into HostGator’s cPanel or DNS management area.
    • Copy all DNS records (A, CNAME, MX, TXT, SPF, DKIM, etc.) into your Route 53 hosted zone.
    • If you use services such as WHM on your current provider, you can use it to export a zone file instead of having to move over records manually. Downloading the zone file may not be possible if you are looking at the DNS records through CPanel.
  • Import DNS Records onto AWS Route53
    • In the AWS Hosted Zone, you will see an import button which you can use to import the zone file provided by the original registrar.
    • You’ll want to make sure services like your website, email (e.g. Google Workspace), SPF/DKIM/DMARC, etc. are correctly replicated.
  • Update Nameservers at HostGator
    • Still inside HostGator’s domain panel, go to the domain settings and replace the current name servers with the 4 NS records from your Route 53 hosted zone.
    • This step points your domain’s DNS to AWS, even though the domain is still registered with HostGator.

DNS changes can take up to 48 hours to propagate, but it’s often much faster (within a few hours).

  • Verify DNS is Working
    • Use a tool like DNS Checker to confirm that your new records are resolving globally.
    • Make sure your website, email, and any other services are still working.

Migrating Domain

Proceed with domain migration once you have confirmed the records have been moved over and that you are getting DNS responses from the new name servers. To actually mover over the domain, all the registrars tend to add several steps in order to ensure the transfers are legitimate and to ensure users are fully informed. All Domain registrars will show settings related to the domain. For example, here is what HostGator shows you:

  • Make sure you meet the following 3 requirements:
    • Make sure the domain is unlocked. Also, it’s important for the original registrar to have your contact information up-to-date, especially the email address.
    • Privacy protection (like WHOIS Guard) should be disabled or the transfer email could go to AWS instead of to the domain owner.
    • It’s important to note that ICANN prevents domains from being transferred if they have been registered within 60 days (or last transferred within 60 days).

  • Request an Auth Code to initiate the transfer.

  • Confirm the transfer request

  • Continue with transfer

  • Send the request to email address on file

  • Wait to receive an email from the original registrar. This can take a few days. HostGator typically takes 3 days to deliver the auth code. After receiving the auth code, you can go to Route 53 / Registered Domains and select the Transfer In button.

  • Route 53 will ask for the auth code at step 2 and then provide pricing for the transfer.

  • After confirming your contact information and submitting the request, the domain transfer can take a few days. Check your inbox for a message from Route53 confirming the move.

Completion

After this, you will be able to see the domain in Route53 under Registered Domains. Going forward, renewals of the domain will be done through AWS. All email notifications / reminders regarding the domain will come from AWS.

entry.title: Deploying a Next.js app to AWS Amplify

link.title: Deploying a Next.js app to AWS Amplify

entry.content:
How to Deploy a Next.js Application Using AWS Amplify

Deploying a web application shouldn’t be a bottleneck—it should be fast, cost-effective, and scalable. If you’re working with Next.js, one of the most popular frameworks for building React applications, there’s no better way to deploy than with AWS Amplify.

In this post, we’ll explore:

  • Why AWS Amplify is a great choice for hosting your Next.js app.
  • How it compares to other options like Vercel, Netlify, and EC2.
  • A simple, step-by-step guide to get your app live with Amplify.

Why Choose AWS Amplify?

AWS Amplify is a powerful platform that automates the deployment and hosting of full-stack web apps. For Next.js developers, Amplify brings several key advantages:

Speed

  • CI/CD built-in: Connect your GitHub repo and Amplify automatically builds and deploys on every commit.
  • SSR support: Amplify natively supports Server-Side Rendering (SSR) and Static Site Generation (SSG) for Next.js apps.
  • Global CDN: Amplify deploys your app to edge locations, ensuring low-latency access around the globe.

Cost Efficiency

  • Pay for what you use: No flat monthly fees. You only pay for build time and hosting bandwidth.
  • Generous free tier: Great for side projects or startups just getting started.
  • No need to manage infrastructure: Unlike EC2 or Fargate, you don’t need to worry about provisioning or scaling servers.

Amplify vs Other Hosting Solutions

Feature AWS Amplify Vercel Netlify AWS EC2
Ease of Setup Easy Very Easy Very Easy Complex
SSR Support Yes Yes Limited Yes
Custom Domains Free HTTPS Free HTTPS Free HTTPS Manual Setup
Build Automation Built-in CI/CD Built-in CI/CD Built-in CI/CD Manual
Pricing Model Usage-based Usage-based Usage-based Pay-per-instance
Scalability Auto-scaled Auto-scaled Auto-scaled Manual scaling

While Vercel (creator of Next.js) is tightly integrated with the framework, Amplify gives you more flexibility with backend services and closer integration with the AWS ecosystem if you already use AWS services like Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, or Cognito.

Step-by-Step: Deploy a Next.js App to AWS Amplify

Here’s how to get your app up and running on Amplify in minutes:

Step 1: Push Your App to GitHub

Ensure your Next.js project is pushed to a Git provider like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.

If not already done:

git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git
git branch -M master
git push -u origin master

Step 2: Log into the AWS Amplify Console

Go to the AWS Amplify Console and click “Create New App”.

Step 3: Connect Your Git Repository

  • Choose GitHub (or your provider of choice) and click on Next.
  • Authenticate with GitHub and select your repository and branch.
  • In the App Settings you will see Service Role, leave it as default: Create and use a new service role

Amplify will auto-detect that you’re using a Next.js app and prefill the build settings.

If you click on Edit YML File, you’ll see a default amplify.yml file like this:

version: 1
frontend:
  phases:
    preBuild:
      commands:
        - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    build:
      commands:
        - npm run build
  artifacts:
    baseDirectory: .next
    files:
      - '**/*'
  cache:
    paths:
      - .next/cache/**/*
      - .npm/**/*

You can tweak this file later if needed.

Step 4: Review and Deploy

  • Click “Next” and review the build settings.
  • Click “Save and Deploy”.

Amplify will:

  • Clone your repo
  • Install dependencies
  • Build your app
  • Deploy it to a globally distributed CDN

Note that Amplify will select an instance type for you.

Step 5: View Your Live Site

Once deployment finishes, you’ll get a public URL like:

https://master.d1234abcd.amplifyapp.com

You can customize the domain by attaching a custom domain in the Amplify Console (e.g., www.myapp.com).

Bonus: Add a Custom Domain

To attach your domain:

  1. Go to the Amplify Console.
  2. Select your app → “Hosting” → “Custom Domains”
  3. Add your domain (e.g., from Route53 or any registrar).
  4. Amplify will configure DNS and SSL for free.

entry.title: From Evernote to Obsidian
entry.content:
Introduction

After over ten years of using Evernote I finally decided to get all my notes out and leave. Evernote was once a great note-taking app but gradually grew into an overgrown, slow, and overpriced solution. Besides the bloat, it always seemed like they kept adding features I didn’t think were core to the product.

Obsidian might seem overwhelming at first, but it only took me a few days to get used to it and I am now a big fan. Obsidian is stronger when used on a non-mobile device, but I am ok with that. The mobile app is still pretty good, and the community plugins really make it shine. I also work mostly out of my desk and prefer using my laptop, especially for note-taking. Also, it turns out that exporting the notes from Evernote into Obsidian was actually rather easy and the conversion process resulted in fairly good results.

Exporting Notes

Evernote allows you to export your notes on a per notebook basis. The resulting .enex files can then be easily imported into Obsidian using the Importer community plugin. The process starts when you right-click on an Evernote notebook and select the Export notebook option:

You can then keep the default values which keep all the attributes selected and uses the .enex format. Clicking on Export will generate the file. You can then repeat this process for all the notebooks.

In Obsidian, the Importer Community Plugin can then be used to import each notebook. After the notes are imported, the Importer plugin can be disabled and you can start reviewing the notes to make sure you are satisfied with the format. In my case, I thought the conversion produced good results and I only had to make some minor adjustments. One particular adjustment, for example, was that some notes which used the # symbol were converted to Obsidian tags, simply putting a backslash character in front of those hash-marks fixed the issue.

Obsidian

If you are a fan of markdown and prefer tools that provide more control of your data then Obsidian is a much better alternative. It has a very rich ecosystem of plugins and also feels a lot lighter as compared to the bloated mess that Evernote became.

entry.title: Hugging Face - The Github for AI

link.title: Hugging Face - The Github for AI

entry.content:
While GitHub has long been the go-to repository for code sharing, version control, and collaboration among developers, Hugging Face has enabled some unique functionality for the machine learning and artificial intelligence community. At first glance, they might seem similar—both support open collaboration and versioning—but Hugging Face is specialized for AI workflows, providing tools and infrastructure specifically for model training, sharing, and deployment.

One of Hugging Face’s standout features is its Models hub, which acts like GitHub’s repositories, but for trained machine learning models. Here, developers and researchers can upload pre-trained models in popular formats like PyTorch, TensorFlow, and ONNX. These models are tagged, documented, and come with metadata such as usage licenses, example scripts, and supported tasks like text classification, image generation, or speech recognition. Users can search for models by task, framework, or language, making it incredibly convenient to find and reuse powerful models without starting from scratch.

The Datasets section on Hugging Face functions similarly to GitHub’s raw data repositories but adds an important layer of standardization and tooling. There is a datasets Python library which simplifies loading and accessing these datasets. This enables anyone to load, preprocess, and explore datasets quickly using familiar methods. Importantly, many datasets are designed to work seamlessly with models on the platform, supporting reproducible research and rapid experimentation.

Perhaps the most innovative part of Hugging Face is its Spaces feature. Spaces are essentially interactive apps or demos built using Streamlit, Gradio, or static HTML, directly embedded within the Hugging Face ecosystem. Think of it as a combination of GitHub Pages and interactive Jupyter notebooks. Developers can showcase their models in action, allowing users to test them out directly in the browser. This dramatically lowers the barrier for non-technical stakeholders or curious users to engage with cutting-edge AI tools, bridging the gap between development and real-world application.

While GitHub remains the gold standard for general software development collaboration, Hugging Face is rapidly becoming the GitHub for AI. It adds layers of domain-specific functionality that cater to the unique needs of machine learning practitioners, including model deployment, dataset management, and demo creation. For developers in the AI space, Hugging Face offers an environment purpose-built for the modern ML lifecycle, making it a true platform for innovation and sharing.

entry.title: Comparing Terraform Version Management Tools
entry.content:
tenv will replace the others

When using Terraform, it’s common to rely on a version manager to easily switch between different versions across projects or environments. For years, tfenv has been the go-to solution in the community. But with the tool seeing little to no active development lately, it might be time to consider more modern alternatives.

Two other tools worth evaluating are tfswitch, a popular option with a user-friendly interactive mode, and the newer tenv, which is quickly gaining traction—especially for teams also adopting OpenTofu, the open-source Terraform fork.

Developed as part of the Tofuutils project, tenv is a Terraform and OpenTofu version manager that was created with today’s infrastructure workflows in mind. It provides the same core functionality you’d expect—installing, switching, and managing versions—but with native support for both Terraform and OpenTofu.

As HashiCorp’s licensing change prompted a surge of interest in OpenTofu, having a version manager that treats both tools as first-class citizens is a major advantage.

Feature comparison

Feature tfenv tfswitch tenv
Active development ❌ No ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Terraform support ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
OpenTofu support ⚠️ Workaround only ❌ Not supported ✅ Native support
Install specific version ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Use .terraform-version ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Interactive version selector ❌ No ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Cross-platform support ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Shell integration (bash/zsh) ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Custom install directory ✅ Yes ❌ No ✅ Yes
Multi-runtime support ❌ Terraform only ❌ Terraform only ✅ Terraform & OpenTofu

entry.title: Initial Configuration of a Dev Environment MacBook

link.title: Initial Configuration of a Dev Environment MacBook

entry.content:
Introduction

After receiving a new MacBook, I usually follow a similar set of steps to get it ready as a development MacBook. Here, I show a list of all the tooling I install in order to get it most of the way there and also the files which should be preserved from one device to the next. This installation works best if performed in the sequence shown.

Steps

The following steps were performed to configure MacBook Pro

  • Make sure XCode is installed, select the components you need:
    • macOS 15.x
    • iOS 18.x
  • Install Chrome
  • Install iTerm2. Make sure to also install shell integration which can be found in the iTerm2 main menu.
  • Install brew
    • See here: https://brew.sh/
    • Homebrew should also install command line tools for Xcode
  • Install wget: brew install wget
  • Install oh-my-zsh
    • See here
  • Install zsh autosuggestions:
    • https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-autosuggestions
    • brew install zsh-autosuggestions
  • Install powerlevel 10K
    • See here
    • Install this plugin to add fonts and nice prompt. Use iterm2. Follow instructions for manual installation, this will install Meslo Nerd Font automatically through iTerm2.
  • Install FZF (fuzzy completion in terminal)
    • See here
    • Use brew to install; then look in the readme for instructions on installing key bindings (such as those for fuzzy auto-completion for CTRL-R)
    • To install useful key bindings and fuzzy completion (after installing fzf via brew):
    • $(brew --prefix)/opt/fzf/install
  • Install zsh syntax highlighting
    • See here
    • Use brew to install: brew install zsh-syntax-highlighting
  • Install VS Code
  • Install Postgres from the website. Don’t use brew
    • Install through downloadable app here
  • Install DBeaver
    • See here
  • Install Docker
    • See here
  • Install bat using brew (bat is an improved version of cat command)
  • Install node and npm using brew
  • Install rbenv, Ruby, and bundler
brew install rbenv
rbenv init
echo 'eval "$(rbenv init -)"' >> ~/.zshrc
# Install Ruby (version 3.2.2)
rbenv install 3.2.2 
rbenv global 3.2.2

# Install bundler
gem install bundler:2.5.7
  • Make sure you have the .vimrc file which has syntax highlighting for vim and also starts NerdTree with the vim command.
  • Install nerdtree:
curl -sS https://webi.sh/vim-nerdtree | sh; \ source ~/.config/envman/PATH.env
  • If necessary, install Terraform using brew
    • See here
  • If necessary, install tfenv using brew
    • Refer to repo
  • If necessary, install AWS CLI
    • See here

Important Files to Preserve

If I am migrating from one device to another, I generally make sure the following files are moved over to the new device:

~/.vimrc

# All SSH keys
~/.ssh/

# The shell history
~/.zsh_history

# I keep all shell alias commands in .alias_list
~/.alias_list

entry.title: Web3 Smart Contracts
entry.content:
Boca Contracts is a platform that allows anyone to deploy Web3 Smart Contracts based on a set of pre-defined templates. Anyone visiting the site can deploy a smart contract to any of several blockchains.

Boca Contracts is a NextJS application that is deployed on AWS via terraform. It is composed of EC2 instances, load balancers, and an RDS database.

The project is made up of the infrastructure code, the front end code, the application itself, and the Solidity contracts. For now, the application holds contracts in Ethereum (mainnet and Sepolia) and BNB Smart Chain.

The finished product can be seen here: Boca Contracts Home Page
